messages.subject: parcelAllocation query
messages.body_plain:
lavaan Users,

I have been running some models using the parcelAllocation function in semTools with lavaan. This implements Sterba and MacCallum's (2010) procedures for assessing item-parcel allocation variability. I have noticed that the fit summary provided by parcelAllocation output gives some strange results.

For example, in all my runs (multiple models with different estimators) CFI average fit comes back as 0.000 as does its standard deviation etc. RMSEA for the same model fit with ML and MLM comes up with wildly different and implausible looking numbers (-151968.0 and 0.926 respectively).

Across all models, the estimator used makes quite a difference to how the values appear, and whether they seem to be in a sensible range for that index. The only fit index which consistently seems to give a) plausible values in the correct range for that index, and b) values I would expect for the models I am fitting, is the TLI.

It is quite possible I have made an error, or that I am misunderstanding these values, but it seems like the function may be pulling the wrong numbers from the lavaan objects. This would make sense, for example, if the lavaan objects are different shapes for the different estimators.

Has anyone else had this problem, or does anyone have any suggestions where I may be going wrong?

Thanks

Tom

Rob

lavaan syntax is just text. So you can generate any pattern of text

# produce all combinations

messages.body_plain:
As with most statistical null-hypothesis tests, the null hypothesis here is that there is no discrepancy whatsoever between the observed sample moments (covariance matrix and mean vector) and those implied by the model, or by implication, that there is no discrepancy between the tested model and the population model that generated the data.  Unless you are testing a saturated model, there will always be some discrepancy, and the p value is the right-tail probability of observing a discrepancy at least as extreme as that between your model and data, given that the null is true.  So larger p-values may indicate that your model fits well (see counter-arguments in http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//0033-295X.107.2.358), and very small ones may indicate poor fit.

However, in social sciences we are never likely to have the correct model (i.e., one that includes all variables that account for a given behavioral phenomenon); rather, we deal with useful approximations.  With large sample sizes (as are typically required for stable estimation in SEM), the chi-squared test is over-powered to detect even trivial discrepancies as statistically significant.  Alternative indices of fit (e.g., RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI) are ways of assessing whether the observed discrepancy is of any practical significance, similar to including a measure of effect size in a t-test or ANOVA.  There are numerous debates about the validity and utility of the chi-squared test and fit indices, for example, the special issue of Personality and Individual Differences, vol 42 (2007).

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill,

What version of R and lavaan are you running?

sessionInfo()

I ran your code on R 2.15.3 with lavaan 0.5-12, and it ran without that warning (and SEs were provided in the summary).

FYI, you don't need to manually specify variances of exogenous predictors in your script when you use the fixed.x = FALSE argument in sem(), and the estimator = "ML" argument is redundant when you specify missing = "fiml" (although I believe you can specify both if you wanted to use FIML with the robust estimator MLR).

Also, there is a function in the semTools package that automates the addition of auxiliary variables in your model so that you don't have to go through extra steps yourself.  You can just specify the simple regression in your script, then include a vector of auxiliary variable names in the call to auxiliary():

employ <- read.table("employee3.txt", header = FALSE)
names(employ) <-c("ID","age","tenure", "female", "well_being", "satisfaction",
                  "performance", "turnover", "IQ")
employ$well_being[employ$well_being == -99] <- NA
employ$satisfaction[employ$satisfaction == -99] <- NA

library(semTools)
?auxiliary

script <- 'performance ~ sat_c + wb_c'
mod1 <- auxiliary(script, data = employ, fun = "sem", aux = c("IQ", "turnover"))
summary(mod1)

You'll notice that the function will create single-indicator latent variables for the observed variables in order to accomplish the saturation of the correlates, but you can see that the corresponding estimates are the same as in the output from your manual model (once you get it to run, perhaps after updating your packages, or R itself).

Terry

Does anyone know if assessing weak (loadings) and strong (thresholds) invariance can be done properly in lavaan?

m1 <- '
f1_1 ~= var1_1 + var2_1 + var3_1
f2_1 ~= var4_1 + var5_1 + var6_1

f2_2 ~= var4_2 + var5_2 + var6_2'

f2_1 ~= f4* var4_1 + f5*var5_1 + f6*var6_1

f1_2 ~= f1*var1_2 + f2*var2_2 + f3*var3_2
f2_2 ~= f4*var4_2 + f5*var5_2 + f6*var6_2'

I cannot reject this test (p=0.943), so loadings would be invariant. Is that conclusion right?

When I use theta parameterization in Mplus (therefore, a different model) I get different conclusions: I cannot support weak invariance.
My Mplus test (allowing free factors means, residual variances, and some restrictions in thresholds for identification) is better or more accurate regarding weak invariance?

Any thoughts, suggestions or references would be very appreciated.
